utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence team of Mr. Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Deirdre Montgomery, and Ivana Batista.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic and Mr. Lennart Poulsen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the Usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for -- for this delay because we were obliged to -- to go through these materials which were more than 30 minutes, so we split our tasks, and we -- we -- we covered everything. Thank you for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. While the witness is on his way in, we propose to sit from -- in two 90-minute sessions which would take us up to the ordinary end of the -- the usual end of the morning sitting at 1.45; and, then, if necessary, we have the afternoon reserved as we would have previously notified. Mr. Traynor, good morning to you. Before I invite Mr. Pantelic to begin his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Traynor. I'm Defence counsel Igor Pantelic for Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. Yesterday you testified about the contact, your personal contact based on your interview with my client, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, at the premises of CSB police building in Banja Luka. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And during that interview, the, I would say, issue or the case of killings of non-Serbs at Vlasic mountain occurred and you discussed that with Mr. Zupljanin, this -- this case.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you -- during your stay in -- in CSB premises, do you recall that you visited other premises like forensic department or criminal investigation department of the Banja Luka police with regard to the same issue, the ongoing investigation with that regard?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you were only in the office of Mr. Zupljanin and you were discussing various issues; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And we saw yesterday, I think it was the -- I don't know exact reference but it was, I think, the last video-clip showed to all of us by the Prosecution and a certain part, I think the author was Ms. Marshall, showing us the work of criminal investigation department and this portion where Mr. Zupljanin showing certain photographs from the scene. Did you see this kind of evidence or materials during your conversation with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the clip you're referring to was not the Marshall ITN material. I think it was the American ABC Nightline report, where they reconstructing and drawing a map and stuff like that. It wasn't on the ITN. I didn't visit any of those places that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you were not shown the relevant photographs, relevant to that case, during your interview with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I believe that you mentioned that -- during your testimony that Mr. Zupljanin, during interview with you, gave you a figure of the victims in Vlasic mountains, non-Serb victims, and I think you mentioned 40 or 50, something like that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we put the figure to him and he said that figure is not right, and he mentioned a figure of around 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And according to your sources and informations, figure was rather higher, like -- around 150 victims?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall being told by an international official in Banja Luka that he been told by the Banja Luka police department that the figure was 188 and that they had confirmed that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we could agree upon the fact that actually the particular investigation related to that massacre on Vlasic was ongoing at the time?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what the police were doing, I mean, that's what I was being told, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because in your previous answer you just mentioned that from police sources, the person from international organisation confirmed that the figure was around 188.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just what I said, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, certain documents speak from -- for themselves, but in order to -- to have a clarity here, Mr. Traynor, I was made certain consultations with client and he recalled that event, that he mentioned that in accordance of his personal and official knowledge, the exact number was around 100 -- more than 140 and that, to that extent, in this previous stage of criminal proceedings, the investigation was -- was launched. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite -- I don't quite understand actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm putting to you is that according to the recollection of my client, during the interview with you he mentioned that it was not 50 victims on Vlasic massacre but rather around 140, at least. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, could we have Exhibit 2D35, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Traynor, on your screen you have Defence exhibit which is document, actually, form of criminal charges in accordance with the relevant law. And these criminal charges are filed on the September -- September 8, 1992. Do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have another page. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, unfortunately, on English version we don't have a seal and a name of the official in charge so we shall -- we are going to ask our friends from translation unit to -- to make necessary translation here. But on the left side, which is a B/C/S document, and you are, as you said, more or less familiar with Serbian language, we see the signature and we see name and family name and function of the person, and it is Stojan Zupljanin, chief of centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's what it looked like to me, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have previous page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As we can see here, Mr. Traynor, the relevant parts of these criminal charges are that there is a description of the events in first paragraph, and then, in the third paragraph, you can see that -- it is actually paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have this page scrolled up, please, just a bit. English version, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it's actually second paragraph from the bottom, where in accordance to the previous informations collected by the criminal investigation department, this is an allegation -- there are allegations that around 140 victims were found at Vlasic Mount. Do you see this part?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So given the fact that these criminal charges were filed on 8th of September, 1992, and you were speaking with Mr. Zupljanin at the end of September, are you now in situation to correct your statement with regard to the number which was, according to you, disclosed during the interview. Because obviously Mr. Zupljanin, who signed these criminal charges, was informed that at least 140 victims were there.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which case I ask myself why he didn't mention the figure 140 to us. Because that's not what I recall. And what's more, he did confirm indeed that there was an investigation being carried out and it was being hampered, and he was asking us, the reporters, the journalists who were travelling in different parts of the country, if we could get in contact with the "Ustashas" in -- on the other side of the line in Travnik and get their assistance because they couldn't complete their investigation. I mean, that's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. Traynor, you were in the, more or less, same situation many times during your stay in the region. Sometimes it is a matter of interpretation so maybe -- if you will allow that possibility that it was just maybe simple mistake of interpretation or understanding of this particular fact, which is a number. Do you allow this possibility?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's always a possibility, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next event that you mentioned in your testimony was -- yes. It's page 11 of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would like to have a clarification on that last question of yours. You asked the witness to allow for the possibility that it was just maybe a simple mistake. What do you mean by a "simple mistake"? Made by the witness, by mishearing what Mr. Zupljanin said or mistake made by Mr. Zupljanin citing the wrong figure?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already -- I -- I -- I put to this witness the position of Mr. Zupljanin in my earlier questions. My particular questions was related to the possibility that -- where interpretation was wrong and that -- that was the actually option that I explore with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the interpretation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Or translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: He misheard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To be precise, Your Honour, it is a translation -- it's a matter of translation from English to B/C/S, because this witness was with -- obviously there with an interpreter, so simply as that, I allow that possibility that it's a matter of translation. Proper translation from English to B/C/S and B/C/S to English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So then let me ask this precisely to the witness, do you allow for the possibility that Mr. Zupljanin said 140 and that you, how -- I -- that you understood 50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding of what's happening here is that Mr. Pantelic is suggesting that there was a translation error or a translation misunderstanding that -- that Mr. Zupljanin was talking about a figure of 140, which I wasn't given, and I was given a figure of around 50. I don't think -- I don't know whether he's inferring that I made the error. I don't believe that I did. It is always, of course, a possibility that there was mistranslation and I -- and, you know, there were mixed communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Next topic, Mr. Traynor, which I would like to discuss with you is related to Celinac incidents, I would say, and you are speaking about this particular incident on page 11 of your -- of your statement dated 8th and 9th of March, 2000, year 2000. Anyhow, you already testified that -- that Mr. Zupljanin said that certain problems, incidents occurred -- occurred in -- in -- in Celinac, where, according to his knowledge, seven Serb soldiers from Celinac were killed at the front line and that possible revenge can be expected. And, finally, at that time it was a fact that actually a number of Muslims killed in Celinac. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that, at the same time, Mr. Zupljanin said that police arrested alleged perpetrators and that certain procedure will be instigated, legal procedure. Now I would like with you to comment on Prosecution exhibit. It's P1279.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have this on our screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So what we can see here, this is an indictment against a number of perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And could we have page 4 of this indictment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Traynor, we see here the first paragraph of the statement of reasons, which is a form of the indictment in accordance with the criminal law at that time, that, on 7th of July, 1992, two Serbs, Sugic Obrenko and Miladin, with the assistance of the other, killed a number of non-Serbs. Do you see that part, please?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I, of course, state that you are not an expert of legal issues, but this is actually an example that the individuals of Serb nationality were arrested, as Mr. Zupljanin mentioned in the interview with you, and that eventually, public prosecutor filed the indictment which is actually the -- the -- the crucial moment for the court criminal proceedings. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean do I agree with you? I'm looking at these league documents for the first time. I've got no idea of the background. So I'm just being presented this and asked to agree with you. The point about Celinac was not about who was killing who or who was murdering who or who was firing guns at who. It was about an official document in the municipality declaring Draconian restrictions on the rights of citizens, and in human rights circles at the time it created a bit of a scandal. And everybody was talking about the parallels with the edicts against the Jews in the Third Reich. That was the issue on Celinac and that's what we were discussing. I was not discussing which particular individual attacked which particular lorry on the 7th of July, 1992, or any other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. But, Mr. Traynor, the point in this case is that police did whatever is necessary in accordance with the law and finally indictment was filed against the perpetrators for this particular accident that you were discussed with Mr. Zupljanin, and that he mentioned it -- that police arrested perpetrators and finally brought them to justice. That's my point. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not really in a position to authentic that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traynor. Next issue is so-called Celinac edict that you mentioned in your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is actually the point where the concept of 92 ter package is -- is actually under big question, because this particular document is not related to the indictment, not related to the municipalities charged by OTP against my client. And 92 ter approach, this is a good example, adopting a package, for example, from Brdjanin case, which was completely other by its nature, is now creating certain -- certain --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Microphone not activated] ... never testified before. There was no 92 ter package for Brdjanin, so I'm not quite sure what -- what your issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My -- my actually reference was to Mr. Krzic package. Because you tendered these particular documents through Witness Krzic, one -- who was testifying in -- in the other case, so that's the problem. Because that case, Brdjanin, is not directly related to this case and now we have to clarify this document. That's my point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So going back to this particular part is -- you said yesterday that, actually, Mr. Zupljanin, during the interview with you, actually confirmed the existence of so-called Celinac edict. That was your words yesterday.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it was no longer in operation and that it was no longer effective, and that was not a denial that it had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that was your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But in your statement from 9th of March, 2000, you, in relation to so-called Celinac edict, you said that, according to your notes and recollection in -- in -- I underlined that, in year 2000, Mr. Zupljanin said the following: "The Celinac document is not available and is practically out of use." Which is completely different, that you are trying to, I would say, add in your testimony yesterday. Where you say --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- where you -- where you just gave your personal conclusion that he actually -- he actually said that he was aware of that document, which is actually not the situation. So, Mr. Traynor, I am putting to you that, number one, Mr. Zupljanin did not tell that you he is aware of the existence of that document; that's point number one. And point number two, I'm putting to you that Mr. Zupljanin said that this is not -- this document cannot be available and it's not available, and there are some, I would say unofficial informations and rumours about that but he is not aware of that particular document. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you at all, no. He said -- my understanding of English is, when you say that something is no longer in use, by definition, it means that it was at one point in use.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's your interpretation, of course. And, tell me, Mr. Traynor, you were -- you were based in the region since 1988. And how many times you actually visited Banja Luka itself?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, overall, in the years since 1988, I would imagine four or five times altogether --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But by 1992, this particular trip that you're talking about was the first time I had been in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And during 1992, later on, did you visit Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you recall how many times and which period?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October, month later, and then off the top of my head at the moment, I would need to think closely. I mean, it was 18 years ago. That was 1992. The war went on until 1995 in Bosnia itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I am just interested in 1992.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, twice, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Being based in the region, Mr. Traynor, you are a quite well-informed journalist about the political events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would say.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My editor seemed to think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are aware of the fact that some -- in the mid of October 1991, in -- in Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, actually, Muslim and Croat parties over-voted Serbian SDS party with regard to the so-called issue of independence. You -- you know?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, yes, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, were you in Sarajevo or elsewhere when -- when -- I'm speaking about the mid of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would imagine I was almost certainly in Croatia. There was a rather, you know, quite hot war raging at the time in places like Vukovar and Dubrovnik and other parts of Croatia, and I was covering that, of course, before I covered the Bosnian war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on the events where -- where in contrary to the -- to the constitutional standards in Bosnia, Croat and Muslim party over-voted Serbian side with regard to the vital interest?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you want me to comment on the politics of Serb Croats and Muslims in Bosnia, in former Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I just want to ask your comments on that particular action instigated by Muslim and Croat part -- party against Serbian party in the Parliament. Do you have any knowledge about the constitutional aspects of this particular action?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have plenty of knowledge about it, but I mean, we were in the process of -- not Bosnia but the socialist Federation of Yugoslavia was in the process of disintegration. Slovenia had gone. Croatia was in the middle of a war, it was already independent, and Bosnia was in the throws of disintegration as well. You had a problem in Kosovo and you had problems eventually in Macedonia, and you had, you know, problems all over this country which was falling apart. So I mean, I really don't think if you are suggesting that the constitution -- what was happening in the -- in the -- in the Assembly in Sarajevo in October 1991 could be taken in isolation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any event you would agree with me that this action -- actually, Mr. Traynor, you were aware about the specific constitutional frame of Bosnia-Herzegovina where three constituent nation created actually Bosnia-Herzegovina? You know about that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you know that that each constituent nation exercises its -- its -- I would say, a right to be protected to -- for their vital interest. You are aware about that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And my question to you is that, are you aware about the fact that in the mid of October 1992, in contrary -- in contrast of vital interest of Serbian -- Serbian nation in Bosnia, two other nations over-voted on an unconstitutional way Serbian part in B and H Assembly. Are you aware or not?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you mean October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: October 1991.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I believe that you have a plenty of informations with regard to the efforts of international community in the course of 1991, but now I'm focussing at the first half of 1992, of various international negotiators, EU representatives, and, of course, US -- US envoys. You are aware about this -- these activities?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to follow it closely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And probably you are aware about the so-called Lisbon Agreement, where, in his capacity of EU envoy, Portuguese diplomat Jose Cutileiro was actually a chairman of this commission in order to find a peaceful solution for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that, at that time, in accordance with the -- I would say, suggestions from international community and also in accordance with the -- certain, I would say, political position of three nations in Bosnia, so-called Lisbon Agreement was -- was -- was created, I would say.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in that agreement, provisions were that Bosnia and Herzegovina will be independent and sovereign state with three cantons run by -- by three -- three people in Bosnia, I would say?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that, suddenly, there are many evidence on that, including former American ambassador in Serbia, Mr. Zimmermann, he is mentioning this particular episode in his book. Suddenly, Mr. Izetbegovic withdrew his consent from that agreement. You are aware about that fact?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know, maybe from your sources or from your personal knowledge, what was motive of Mr. Izetbegovic to withdraw his consent from that particular -- particular, I would say, basic agreement, important agreement for Bosnia. Do you have any informations about this episode?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got lots of opinion but I've got really no idea. I mean, it is very difficult to say. You know, this is a convoluted and complicated and extremely long, you know, difficult thing to sum up in a sentence. He could have thought he was getting a bad deal. He could have thought it wouldn't work. He thought it could have failed. He could have been promised other stuff from other major powers, all sorts of reasons. But if the fundamental kind of point that you seem to be making, if I understand you properly, is perhaps you think that the Serbs got a raw deal here, given that they were constituent nation in the Republic of Bosnia, and if that's your point, I would tend to agree with you. In Yugoslavia generally, of course, in the collapse of this country, the Serbs had an argument. They had a strong case in what would happen to the Serbs in Croatia and what would happen to the Serbs in Bosnia, what would happen to the Serbs in Kosovo. These are all legitimate and totally warranted concerns. The problem is when you get into a war, if you have an argument, it is how you prosecute your argument, and you can also, in my view at least, you can invalidate your case by the way you prosecute it. And that's exactly, in my view, what happened. Basically, the means obliterated the end. Basically because, you know, the way they behaved and the actions that they took, they lost the moral argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, in general terms, of course, I -- I -- I cannot but agree with you. But in criminal cases, actually, are we are dealing with the individual responsibility and we are not going in such a broad -- broad, I would say, space. But --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't me that raised the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, what I would like to point out with you is that, maybe you are aware or not, but in accordance with Lisbon Agreement, each, I would say, constituent unit will have in this new created Bosnia-Herzegovina its own police forces. Are you aware about that fact?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, finally, in 1995, the crown of international mediation and efforts, peaceful efforts, Dayton Peace Accord actually was signed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it's a fact of common knowledge that in accordance with this particular international document two -- I would say, two -- two constituent units of Bosnia-Herzegovina created Republika Srpska and Bosnian actually -- actually Muslim-Croat Federation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, with its -- both of these units, they have their own jurisdiction over the police and they have their own governments. Of course, certain, I would say, certain part of -- of power was transferred to the -- to the -- to the common -- common organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Traynor, I would like to ask you a few questions about the -- your -- your -- about your yesterday's testimony and your comments on related to -- to Prijedor area, Kozarac area, et cetera. First of all, Mr. Traynor, when you gave your comments on the Kozarac village with regard to the destruction, do you allow possibility that this kind of destruction was a result of -- of armed conflict and clashes in the region?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there at the end of May 1992 when the place was, you know, destroyed. Everything that I had been told about it was that it was surrounded and shelled, also by outsiders, by international people that investigated what happened there, that it was surrounded by Serbian forces and it was mercilessly shelled with the people -- with the civilian population still in their houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And did you collect certain informations with regard to the Muslim armed forces in the region, in time -- in that time, May or June 1992? Do you have any knowledge about the -- the -- the size of -- of their forces?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I suggest to you that in the region of Kozarac and Prijedor at least 3.000 Muslim armed soldiers were operating, would you accept this proposition?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to, you know, take you at your word. I mean, I can't accept it or reject it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But well, I -- I would be grateful to you to explain us. When you -- when you come to certain information, do you have a process to double-check it? For example, if you saw Kozarac area destroyed, did you -- did you ask some Serb military officials what was going on in that area, I mean, in terms of, I would say, balanced -- balanced approach? Did you have any contact with Serbian military officials with that regard?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Kozarac, and I was almost arrested by Serbian military officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well -- well, I'm not -- it was not my -- my understanding that these soldiers, I would say, and guards are officials. My question to you is: Did you try to obtain informations from General Talic who was a commander of the region at the time?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you try to obtain information about the combat activities in the region from, I don't know, a military commander of the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So simply, you just passed through the region of Kozarac. You collected certain informations from -- from -- from non-Serb refugees with regard to the events in Kozarac, and you actually wrote your story, which is an article. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But, actually, you wrote your story without any particular voice or informations from the other warring party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also spoke to other people, international people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, please.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- officials --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Traynor, my question is very straightforward. I'm asking you, you did not actually write your article on the basis of informations, potential informations that you could collect from Serbian military officials. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, no. A town of 15.000 been razed and levelled, and the entire population had been emptied, and I spoke to dozens of people from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you as a -- I mean, you're a well-educated and quite intelligent person.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You allow the possibility that certain armed conflict between two sides occurred at that time in the region of Kozarac and Prijedor. Is it --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there was some return fire, yes. Armed conflict is a relative term.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So practically you are not in situation to make a fair conclusion whether destruction was a part of legitimate war operation headed by army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about. A legitimate war operation where you surround a town of 15.000 civilians and bomb them, is that a legitimate war operation? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. I'm putting to you, Mr. Traynor, that it might be a case that during a war, legitimate war conflict and operation, certain houses, certain -- certain property was destroyed. Do you allow that possibility?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And do you allow possibility that, in accordance with the military regulations and military law, the measure introduced by the -- a warring party, by the -- by the -- by the military unit, to evacuate civilians that could be a case. Yes?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my experience, no, or observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But were not present at Kozarac in May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it's just your, I would say, speculation, with regard to the --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- particular events?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would say it was much, much stronger than -- I would say it was not speculation, no. It was in-depth reporting and trying to establish and recreate and reconstruct what happened there. If just because you have been [indiscernible] in 1945, doesn't mean to say you can't find out what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Traynor, let's conclude this topic with the following conclusion. You were not there in Kozarac in 1992. You allow the possibility that in accordance with the certain military operation, certain consequences for civilians might be done, and that you wrote your articles on the basis of one side source. Am I correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, you're not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and you're trying to put words in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traynor. You will have a possibility to explanation in re-direct whatever you want. This is a -- this a --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the witness must be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: -- answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, and no. This is an cross-examination. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Sorry, Your Honour. Sorry, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm simply asking that the witness be given an opportunity to answer one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The last question you asked Mr. Pantelic, has the witness answered it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He said he is not agree with me, but ... he said -- I said yes or no. He said, "I am not, and you're trying to put words in my mouth," end of story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And you were interrupting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because he is starting to give his comments. And in the cross-examination I am perfectly entitle -- because I'm conducting the cross-examination and -- and -- and the witness, and in re-examination, Your Honour, the Prosecution can -- can ask everything which is along the line of the -- of the -- of the cross-examination. That's my point. So I put -- I'm putting a leading questions. I -- it is my strategy which kind of questions I will put, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And you should draw the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I'm asking for answers. I am entitled to have answers yes or no, do you agree with me or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The short of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... because Mr. Pantelic has got it on. Thanks. Your Honours, that's not right. It may be what the American system is, but the British, Canadian, Australian system and most systems allow the witness to give the answer in response to the question. It cannot be cut off, provided it is a relevant answer. And that's the difference. So Mr. Pantelic is not correct in saying he can just tell the -- instruct the witness to answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, as usual, all the other part of the world against United States, that's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I'm sorry, but I'm not -- I'm not into the American or the English or the whatever, but what I do resent is that you asked the -- you put to the witness that he is -- he wrote his article on -- on the basis of one source only. He said no and he wanted to explain what his other sources were, and you just shut him down. I don't think it is acceptable. Not in my system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you may be right, but this witness already gave the answer to that particular question. He said that he wrote his article from the source of international community officials and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So if he gave that answer already, why did you -- why do you put to him, then, that he didn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In order to save judicial economy, Your Honour, because we already got this answer and I anticipated what the answer would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then let the witness give his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Traynor, let me have a certain -- certain conclusion. You did not write your article on the basis of Serbian military officials information. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you stated earlier that you wrote your article on the basis of the information that you collected from -- from non-Serb refugees as well as from certain international organisation official sources. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Judge Delvoie, I think it is clarified the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, now let's go to your opus, your journalist opus in -- which I find, I mean, in total, very, very fruitful, but now I'm focussing on year 1992. We have been provided by the Prosecution four pages of articles in 1992, and I stand corrected, in total it's a list of 170 newspaper articles. You agree with me? In 1992.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring to Bosnia, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, referring to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't know, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The work and the activity and the profession of a journalist is, I would say, a rather creative activity. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what you mean by creative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean the -- my understanding of -- of -- of -- of that particular work is that, based on certain analytical activities, collections of informations, you are actually trying to -- to -- to inform your readers on the basis of what information you collected.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Creative, of course, has different meanings. It can mean that you're making things up. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, of course, to achieve a certain standard of -- of -- of objectivity, a professional journalist will act in accordance with certain professional standards, among which, when writing or transferring certain information, it should be confirmed from various sources, at least two. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, yes, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, usually. But if, for example, certain matter of urgency is a priority, then you are just sending your information from the field -- field without any -- any other confirmation. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no. It depends, I mean, it's -- it's a varied menu. You know, you -- I can see what you're inferring, but, of course, you try -- it depends on the kind of information you're supplying. And, of course, you try and corroborate stuff with a second, and third, and fourth, and fifth sources. You can also be witnessing things and seeing things directly, and you're writing about them. You don't need to confirm that with anyone else. For example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to have your comments as a -- really, a well-known journalist. We have a situation in -- in -- in Bangkok with the red shirt protestors. I mean, at the moment when protest started, you were there in the street, and my understanding that you will simply send information and -- and you will report that something is going on on the streets of Bangkok, without entering into the cause. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, entering into what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the first moment that you are personal -- that are you testifying that something is around you. I mean, without any previous knowledge that something will occur. You are just walking on the streets, you see the clashes, and then you are reporting to your -- to your headquarter that something is going on those streets, without entering into the cause and the issue. I mean, in details. Am I right? That's your instinct as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It should be.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, you're not right. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. Could you explain how --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if you were in Bangkok right now and then there is riots on the street and you happen to be there as a reporter, the chances are that you've been in Bangkok for quite a while. You're supposed to know something about the politics of country that you're in. You are perfectly aware there's been a political crisis in Bangkok for the past -- in Thailand for the past two years, and all of that informs what you're witnessing. So you don't just write a report that says, Oh, somebody threw a petrol bomb in Bangkok.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. In the case of Bosnia, practically you were there, you were collecting informations, and you will actually writing your articles and sending your reports on the basis of various sources. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But, of course, during your stay in the region, I mean, Bosnia, you were informed about the -- it was March 1992. You were informed about the tragic accidents committed by Croat soldiers against Serb civilian population in northern Bosnia in the village of Sijekovac. Do you know this tragic episode?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During your stay in the region, I mean, Bosnia, you were aware about the attack on JNA convoy in Sarajevo which occurred the end of April, beginning of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I do apologise if I cause certain technical problems. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, of course, you are aware that recently in -- in -- on the basis of -- of Interpol arrest warrant alleged -- allegedly head of that operation against JNA soldiers in Sarajevo, Mr. Ejub Ganic arrested in UK, and he's still there waiting for the extradition procedures to be finalised?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. I'm not sure, I think he might -- I'm not sure if he is still in the UK, but, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, please, in the list of your articles, did you -- did you write about that attack on -- on JNA soldiers in Sarajevo? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And being in Bosnia, do you recall the incidents which is also a part of -- of -- of court proceedings against JNA soldiers in Tuzla, town of Tuzla. Do you know something about this incident?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which particular incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where Muslim forces attacked JNA soldiers during their process of -- of -- of transportation out of Bosnia and certain serious casualties occurred, do you know [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult -- it is a difficult at a distance of 18 years to remember every single incident that happened in a three-year, three-and-a-half-year Bosnian war, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm just focussing on the events in 1992, and I'm just referring to major sort of incidents where Serbian sites were -- was a victim. Simply as that. I'm just covering this -- this -- this particular, major well-known incidents. In your -- during your interview with Mr. Zupljanin, and you are mentioning that in your statement and also in your yesterday's testimony, he mentioned that it was a few days ago, before your -- your interview with him, in village of Serdari, it is a Kotor Varos municipality. Serbian civilians were attacked by Muslim forces, and they were killed, and among them a couple of -- of young children, aged 3 or 4 years, and elderly people, more than 70 years, were killed. Do you remember that particular part of the interview that you have with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And actually it was not of your particular interest to -- to report on that event or to make an article about that.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you explain us why?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I wasn't there interviewing Mr. Zupljanin to research an article about the village of Serdari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Actually, you were not interested in this particular story because your editors directed you to -- to produce and to -- to -- to -- to work only on the stories where Muslims were victims. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're completely, 100 per cent wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But -- I mean, you will describe yourself as a good professional, good journalist, very balanced and objective. Am I right? I mean, if you would qualify yourself as a professional. Or maybe --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is for others to judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest, very, very soon, how I understand your work. But tell me, Mr. Traynor, is there any word or article in the list of 170 articles that you made in Bosnia in 1992, which is a list in front of us, can you indicate any single article reporting and speaking about the atrocities against Serbian population? Can you give me a simple example?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The witness might be -- if you provided him with a list, he may be able to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would be really happy. Mr. Smith, do you have copy, or I can give my -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's time for the break. I wonder if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Oh. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry this is taking so long, but it's difficult to tell just from the headlines, but on the surface, it doesn't look like there are any. Plenty of stories from Serbia, of course, lots of stories from Belgrade, lots of stories about Serbian politics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean, take your time. I don't have problem during the break. But in -- I mean, I didn't find any article made by you about Serb victims. That's the problem, Mr. Traynor. That's the problem. And you can write of any other political events in the region, et cetera, but I'm specifically asking you, do you have any article produced by you in 1992 with regard to Bosnia events where you were writing about Serbian victims. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very many in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, Mr. Traynor, I am suggesting to you, there is not a single article made by you with regard to the Serbian victims. That's my --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's my position.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I remember driving -- for example, off the top of my head, I remember driving into Sarajevo at one stage, driving through a fire-fight on the road from Belgrade. I didn't know where I was, didn't know which side of the line I was on, had to take cover. I was in a village and I was with Serbs who were being attacked, and I wrote about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, I mean, my question was -- was very, very straightforward. I'm not speaking about your chats, about your drinking rakija or, you know, gathering with Serbian soldiers and Serbian friends. No. I'm not speaking about cevapcici. I'm not speaking about your nice time in the region. Mr. Traynor, what I'm asking you, to indicate in the list provided to us by the Prosecution, list of your articles, a single example where you wrote about Serb victims on the basis of your knowledge and your sources in Bosnia in 1992. Please, do you have this information or no? Yes or no, and let's move to the other topics. Please.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered you. I said I don't recall any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what is our timing today. Is it about time for the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Ah, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So being in Banja Luka for these couple of days, and previously being in Croatia, I am almost sure that you were informed about the significant number of Serbian refugees in the region of Banja Luka coming from Croatia and elsewhere from Bosnia. Am I correct with this assessment?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The -- well, main reason I would like to -- to hear your comment, of course, the main reason for this flow of -- of Serb refugees in the region of Banja Luka was caused by the war operation in -- in -- in Croatia. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also the other, I would say, part of -- of that flow of Serbian refugees in the region of Banja Luka caused by the clashes and -- and -- and war operations in the Muslim- and Croat-controlled territory in Bosnia. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of any big flow of refugees in that direction -- from that direction, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you want to tell us that, actually -- you want to tell us that actually Serbs were living freely and with all -- with respect of their rights in the Muslim- and Croat-held territory in Bosnia. Is that your assessment or your confirmation?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was certainly a lot of Serbs living freely in Sarajevo, that's for sure. Who chose to live there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You want to tell us that, speaking of Sarajevo, of course, you want to tell us that during the war a significant number of Serbs were living freely in Sarajevo under the Muslim-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when was the last time that you visited Sarajevo recently?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah, recently.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, still, lot of Serbs are living there, according to your informations?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, you know, I mean, the Serbian forces separated Sarajevo, and at the end of war, in 1996, they organised a mass exodus of -- of as many Serbs as they could muster out of Sarajevo. I remember that, after the Dayton conference agreement. During the war, which is what we were talking about I think, there were plenty of Serbs living in Sarajevo, including politicians, including military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's really a new information for us, and you are really of great assistance to give us completely new aspect of that life. Of course, the facts are against your assessment. But speaking of this organised exodus, would you agree with me when I put to you that actually in accordance with the Dayton Peace Accord, Serbian-held territory of Sarajevo was actually left to -- to Muslim side. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the peace agreement, yes. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that this particular exodus is related to the movement of Serbian -- Serbian people from previously Serbian-held territory of Sarajevo. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may be correct, but you are asserting -- you're asserting your own facts. I don't share your assessment of what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Actually you're surprising me with your findings, I would say. Well, on the other hand, it's -- you are very cooperative for Defence case with your statements. So you want to tell us here, Mr. Traynor, that Serbs lived peacefully, without any problem, in the Croat- and Muslim-held territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that your information that you want to --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the various --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, this line of question is not related to tu quoque. It is just a concept and I'm relating to -- I'm relating to the -- to some extent credibility of this witness, so I'm not going explore in bigger terms these issues so be -- be relaxed that I'm not to go through all this stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Traynor, you -- I mean, your conclusion is that, actually in this tragic civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that actually Serbs are, I would say, main actor or perpetrator of all these atrocities. I'm speaking about the relations between Serbs, Croats and Muslims in Bosnia. What is your personal assessment?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I feel again that words are being put in my mouth. But in any case, I don't share your fundamental premise. I don't think it was a civil war in the first place, so I would rather, you know, emphasise that these are -- this is not my opinion. In the period in question which speaking you're about and in relation to the fact that there don't appear to be any articles from 1992 about Serb victims, the fact of the matter is that in the war in Bosnia, between April and November 1992, the war was effectively over by then, and it was controlled 65, 66, two-thirds, by Serbian forces within that six-month period. Sarajevo was under siege. Eastern Bosnia had been cleansed. Roughly 2 million people had been uprooted from their homes. The overwhelming majority of those people were Bosnian Muslims. And in the west of the country, of course, you had tremendous tensions between Croats and Muslims, and it was not a nice place for Serbs to be living either, whether in Mostar or in other parts of central Bosnia. And, of course, there was plenty of Serbian victims there. The fundamental direction in 1992 was one of the superior Serbian forces taking control of large -- more than half of Bosnia and hundreds of thousands of people, predominantly Bosnian Muslims, being forced to leave homes, and one is reflecting that during one's work during this period. When you're covering a war, if a capital city of Europe is under siege, you tend to write about it from the point of view of the victims. That's what the world wants to hear about, that's what editors want to know about. And similarly, if you are, you know, travelling with UN forces or aid convoys, et cetera, and you can see who is getting the aid, and how it's being blocked, and who is not getting it, and who is doing the blocking, et cetera, et cetera, one tends to write about it from that point of view. That is what we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of -- of -- of this personal assessment, actually, you started to write one-sided articles during 1992. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not one-sided articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are reflecting the reality on the ground. That is not -- it would be one-sided to be doing it the other way around. The reality on the ground is that one side is taking control of more than half of the country and creating a -- killing a lot of people and creating an awful lot of victims in the process, and in fact, what is routinely called one-sided is actually an accurate reflection of the reality of Bosnia in the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Traynor, that was the gist of my question to you. You consider Serb side as a dominant in this conflict and as a main, I would say, in general terms, perpetrator against non-Serbs. That's your personal position. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the -- they -- the war was virtually over by November. Next three years were just basically --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Please I'm asking for your personal position with regard to who is the main perpetrator of the crimes in Bosnia in 1992. Your personal position, please.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I am aware, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes or no. I mean, I'm suggesting you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand the thrust of your questions over the last 15 minutes or so, seeking to indicate the lack of objectivity, my words, you used the word "bias," on behalf of the witness. But when you narrowed it down to asking his opinion, remember he is not being called as an expert. He is tendered by the Prosecution as a witness to give his observations, and whereas those observations would have included certain incidental conclusions, we must draw the line when you're asking directly his opinion because it is really irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you, Your Honour. Is it the time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Any idea how much longer you expect that you would be with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As I just answered my learned friend Ms. Korner, depending of my inspiration. But I would say I would try to do that in maximum half an hour, even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But it will depend on the answers of the witness, you know, on some evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, earlier you -- during your quite lengthy answer, you mentioned that you do not agree with me when I stated that there was a civil war in Bosnia. But, of course, Mr. Traynor, you're not a legal expert. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And probably you are not aware of the findings in Samac case, where I was a Defence counsel, where the Prosecution theory with regard to the international aspect of that completely failed. You are not aware about this judgement?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where are we going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are going just in the middle of the role of press in conflict and certain personal, I would say, information with that regard. With regard to the figures, with regard to the process of spinning up things because this witness yesterday mentioned in his testimony that he -- he was a witness of certain -- certain process of -- of spinning the -- the -- the informations that -- that's -- I would like to -- to explore with him. It was the answer on the question of Ms. Pidwell yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then move directly to that topic because the question of whether there was an international or internal conflict doesn't appear to be conducive to questioning the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, because he just mentioned that from his point of view it's a civil war. Just I want to clarify that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Traynor, tell me, are you aware of the article, I think it was in "New York Times" or "Washington Post", I think it was published sometimes in 1993 or 1994, about the alleged persecution of 17.000 non-Serb -- non-Serb population from area of Samac, northern Bosnia. Are you aware of that article?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that, as you mentioned earlier in your testimony during the examination-in-chief -- well, you can confirm, can't you, that the -- the -- the mechanism during conflicts for producing certain information and to -- to achieve certain goals is actually a process of spinning informations, in terms of achieving certain goals.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am speaking about -- to be more specific, I'm speaking about so-called media war during the war in Bosnia, practically each side -- this is a part of the conflict and elsewhere, each side of warring -- each warring party would like to present its own -- its own truth, I would say.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's been plenty of studies of the role of the media in the disintegration of Yugoslavia. I mean, I could recommend, for example, "Forging War" by Mark Thompson. It's a book written on the subject. There's no --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a consensus view that the media played a strong role in the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was exactly my point, especially speaking of the Bosnia arena. You would agree with me, would you not, that's also that's a case also with domestic and -- I mean, local media and international media. I mean, same -- same -- same system applies, I would say. You would agree with me --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You aware of the fact that, in 1992, a number of 200.000 Muslim women was raped. That was a fact which was circulated in -- in -- in international circles in the area, something like that.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the exact figure. I mean, it's been well established, including in this Tribunal, I think, that, you know, that -- that rape was used as a weapon of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I'm speaking about figures. So you are not aware of numbers at the time?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are very difficult figures to corroborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because you said - correct me if I'm wrong - that how many, 2 million Muslims in -- in Bosnia -- or from Eastern Bosnia moved out from the territory. Is that what -- the gist of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that 2 million, according to UNHCR, were uprooted. Not all of them were Muslims but the majority were. In Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because my understanding was that you referred only to Muslim population. Now you clarified that, and -- yes, thank you. About the victims, total number of victims in war conflict in Bosnia, can you -- can you give us your personal knowledge about the number?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most kind of detailed and forensic examination that I'm aware of into the deaths in Bosnia was run by a man called Tokaca, in Sarajevo, funded by -- I think by the Danish government. And he did a fairly painstaking examination and came up with a figure of just under 100.000, I think, with about two-thirds of the dead being, again, Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean, we all agree that a victim is a victim no matter which nationality and these are tragic consequences of the war. But, Mr. Traynor, can you tell us which figures of -- of -- of -- I'm specifically asking you of Muslim victims, circulated in -- in 1992 in international community and in journalist community, I would say. Can you recall that number?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was all sorts of figures being bandied around at the time. It was too early.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With regard to the -- your -- your contacts in Banja Luka in this particular period, you testified that -- first of all, let me -- let me ask you a -- another question. Could you tell us, please, if it not -- not within your -- I would say, certain security obstacles. I'm not asking, Mr. Traynor, to hear about the names of your sources, like -- like some international officials, international -- and, please, I would like to ask you, during your stay in Banja Luka the names of -- of officials with whom you -- you spoke or you -- you -- you collect certain informations or made interviews. You mentioned Mr. Zupljanin. Did you speak with -- were you able to speak with General Talic, who was the commander of that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate us or could you -- could you give us other -- other names of -- of -- of -- I would say, sort of -- not high rank but upper-ranked officials that you were contacted at the time, no matter of which nationality. Can you give us?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic, Radovan Karadzic, for example. David Owen, Lord Owen. The head of the UNHCR in Banja Luka at the time, Robin Zebuk [phoen]. People from the International Committee of the Red Cross. Off the top of my head that's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All of these persons that you just mentioned, you conducted interview with them?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean, in the formal interview?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not always formal interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I take it that with -- with Mr. Karadzic you spoke unformally about the quality of beer or stuff like that, or maybe your further -- that -- that I found in your statement. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So the beer was the topic with him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the only topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The issue, maybe. Okay. So could you tell us, please, Mr. Traynor, apart of this persons, I would say, high -- high-ranked officials that you just mentioned, can you indicate another individuals that you contacted in Banja Luka during this stay?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, lots of individuals. You're asking about high-ranking officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking for -- I think you mentioned that you were in contact with the local political leaders in Banja Luka. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the meeting with -- between the political leadership and Vance and Owen, so it was an easy opportunity to talk to people, so you could talk to people like Karadzic and Owen at these meetings, plus Mr. Zupljanin, plus lots of people -- ordinary people living in Banja Luka, plus the international aid community and relief workers there at the time. In a matter of three or four days, I mean, that's, you know, quite a full agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were in contact with the HDZ political leader in Banja Luka, I mean, Croat party leader. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe you were in contact with the SDA political leader in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Muharem Krzic, yes, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And before that period that you were in Banja Luka, did you -- did you have any -- any previous contact with him or ...

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And later?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And were you able to contact or to be -- to be -- to be -- to try to interview or to -- to -- to get some informations from Serbian political leader in Banja Luka that you just mentioned before. I think Mr. Vukic who was the president of SDS party in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for interviews with the local political leaders, and we were granted an interview with Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who you ask to be -- to be granted with the ...

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The press service. I don't exactly recall. We put in requests for interviews. That's how we ended up interviewing Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case you requested contact with SDS political leader, I think --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah. You were testifying yesterday about the police presence in -- in Banja Luka, and according to your assessment, you found that it was quite odd to have a number of police officers on the street of Banja Luka. Am I correct? Again, you can --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I mean it's -- I'm constantly having my own words -- you know, words put into my mouth. I didn't say it was odd. I said there was a lot of police on the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which is an absolutely usual -- usual thing, when it's a time of war.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't believe - correct me if I'm wrong - that you wrote an article on the basis of the information that you collected from -- from SDA chief, political SDA chief in Banja Luka. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There would have been information included from him in the article, not on the basis of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean, it was long time ago, but what -- what actually was the -- the -- your, I would say, description of certain events in Banja Luka based on?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have a reference to the article that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not referring, I'm just asking witness whether he -- he mentioned this informations. I actually -- that's the first time that -- that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I heard and I'm reading that you were asking about: "... an article on the basis of information you've collected from the SDA chief, political SDA chief in Banja Luka.
