Am I right?" You wrote an article on the basis of the information received from this man. I'm asking for the reference to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Traynor? What was the article --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: No. I'm asking for a reference from you, because I'm assuming that you have read the article, if you're putting it to him in that form.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, with particular issue, I was just trying from witness to confirm that fact, whether he wrote article or not. He just said that yes, he -- he -- he wrote that article. And I'm ... yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the article's probably been submitted. I'm sure Muharem Krzic is mentioned in at least one of the articles I wrote at the time. It's very easily established. I mean, I don't have it here to hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. My point, Mr. Traynor, is the following. Actually I'm not speaking by your article itself. I'm speaking about your recollection of the certain descriptions or event in Banja Luka at that time. So could you -- could you tell us what was the gist, I would say, of your conversation with -- with gentleman that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly but it will be reflected in the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What's the point, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm asking this witness -- okay. Let me rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, do you have any personal knowledge of the security situation in Banja Luka at the time when -- when you were there in September or October? I mean, based on your various sources?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of people that we were speaking to, the international aid workers or relief workers who were running around at their wits' end, trying to organise convoys and accompany convoys, and bus-loads and truck-loads of people criss-crossing the entire region at the time by the dozen, looking for somewhere to go, this is what we were being told by the people who were on the ground monitoring it, including the local SDA leader who had been to the railway station; for example, when trains were being taken full of refugees to the front line, I think at Maglaj or Doboj, as I recall off the top of my head. Diplomats in Belgrade were aware of the situation. I spoke to them, and on the basis of -- I spoke to people who were -- had police cars on the streets and loud-speakers, and they were being ordered out of their homes and they'd be taken out and they'd be told to walk to the other side of the road. And a little while later, they'd be told to return to their homes, and they'd find this rather frightening and terrifying, et cetera. That was the information based on first-hand interviewing in Banja Luka that I was given at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Traynor, I kindly ask you to speak a bit slower due to the efforts of our interpreters and for the benefit of the court recording. Thank you. So, yeah, what I would like to ask you is the following. During this state of war in Banja Luka when -- I mean, you were there in -- a couple of times in the second part of 1992. You would agree with me, would you not, that actually Krajina region was just the edge of the front line, with lot of battles going around. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you agree with me, would you not, that due to the -- the -- the heavy presence of -- of military personnel and all other armed unit, a serious security situation in Banja Luka was -- was -- was affected -- I mean, seriously affected due to the presence of armed units and individuals. Would you agree with me, with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't my sense of Banja Luka, the city, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your quest for information -- for -- for -- for the sources and information, were you aware that in first nine months in Banja Luka, actually, police recorded and -- and filed criminal charges in number of 5.294 criminal acts. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that during these first nine months of 1992 in Banja Luka, police actually resolved 55 per cent of all recorded criminal acts? Are you -- were you aware of that fact at the time?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And were you aware of the fact that at that time 50 -- I mean, speaking of first nine months of -- of 1992, that 50 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must object. This witness wasn't here, in Banja Luka, for the first nine months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: He testified that his first visit to Banja Luka was in September 1992. I fail to see where this line of questions is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pidwell, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Yeah, yeah. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I think it is inappropriate that he be asked to comment on things that he has not testified about and has no knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Traynor, is a professional journalist so I am just exploring the area of his work in Banja Luka. If one could assume if -- if a professional journalist is going to collect certain information, in certain area, probably he would be able to ask officials about the security situation. Because with -- with -- with political leader in -- in Banja Luka, Mr. Traynor said that he collected a number of informations regarding the security. So I'm now asking this witness to confirm, or not, his personal knowledge about the facts. And I'm just getting to get these answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I'm sorry, but it seems to me that throughout your cross-examination of this witness you have been very indirect in your questions and the effect of it -- of this is, that we are not going ahead very quickly. So I would, actually, appreciate if you would go head on with your questions to the witness and put them directly to him rather than beating around the bush, as it seems to me that you have been doing most of the time. The Presiding Judge reminded the parties yesterday that the Chamber is fully aware of the profession of this witness, that he is a journalist, and we will assess his testimony in light of that fact. So you don't have to make it more difficult than necessary to get directly to the points that you wish to make. Be -- please be more direct and -- and quicken up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will -- yes. I will try to -- to -- to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Traynor, during your stay in Banja Luka, did you get certain informations about the judicial and -- and court proceedings, I mean, investigation against political leader of SDA in Banja Luka and the other members of his group, with regard to the conspiracy and armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During your conversation with the police officials, Mr. Zupljanin and others maybe, did you came to the information that Muslim charity organisation Merhamet was involved in military organisation and preparation for the resistance and the insurgence in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you try to -- to verify this information from the other sources? Did you discuss that issue with -- with some other sources maybe?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also discussed with it Krzic. I never wrote about it, but I discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of Mr. Krzic with that regard?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite predictable. That that wasn't happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So I take it you are not aware that in 1994 there was criminal proceedings against these people before the military court in Banja Luka. You are not aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see how I could be aware of something that happened two years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean now.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that in your interview with Mr. Zupljanin he said that the main reason for -- for people to -- to -- to -- to leave the territory in the wartime period, according to him, was actually economic reasons. You -- you remember that part?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of -- or maybe you can comment, or maybe you can give us the figures, how many refugees from -- from -- from Bosnia actually left country to -- to -- to third -- third countries?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this is a test of my expertise or a kind of quiz game or something, but I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case, this is a fact of common knowledge that I'm not now not speaking of the nationality of the refugees, I'm speaking about the refugees no matter of nationality including, I mean, Serbs -- Serb refugees, Croat refugees, as well as Muslim refugees. So you would agree with me, would you not, that a significant number of them are still living in third countries and they are not returning to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what is the reason for that? There is no war in Bosnia now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How can the witness possibly answer that question. He is seeking an opinion from him, he is not an expert. It is not relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking your opinion, Mr. Traynor. I would like to ask you as a professional journalist. You know, writing about the -- the events in Bosnia and in this present period, did you come to certain informations with regard to the issue why refugees are not returning back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Once again he is seeking his opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll say -- I mean, I'm not a sociologist, and there are very, very complicated reasons why this might be the case. What I do know is that what Mr. Zupljanin told me, of what I do remember, is that these were economic migrants that were leaving for a better life. They would prefer to get 400 Deutschemarks a day and stay in a German hotel, and that he was organising transports with dignity. Judging by what I was seeing around me, I found this extremely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. But would you agree with me, as I said, that a number of all three nationalities, refugees, left Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an objective fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And during your stay in the region, I'm specifically speaking about year 1992, I mean, what is your informations with regard to the significant number of -- of workers leaving former Yugoslavia and working elsewhere in Europe, like in Germany, et cetera. Are you aware of that fact? I mean --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, where on earth are we going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my client, during the conversation with Mr. Traynor, gave his opinion with regard to the motives of a number of people leaving territory as refugee. So now I just want to explore this fact with the witness and his personal knowledge about the factors in the region. Historical and economical. Simply as that. On the basis of his personal knowledge, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, honestly, Mr. Pantelic, the reasons why refugees from the former Yugoslavia have not returned to their homes are, first of all, not relevant to the trial, as far as I can tell, and are way beyond the knowledge of Mr. Traynor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Furthermore, Mr. Pantelic, if I may, the witness gave you the answer to your question, so perhaps we could move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, I would like to put to you that -- actually, prior to that, would you -- would you give me your personal knowledge and comment on the way how -- I would say, form of how you -- you -- you prepared your articles during your stay in -- in Bosnia in 1992. Actually, what I'm interested in is that I would like to know, did you work by yourself or -- or -- or it was a kind of office that you have, with various assistants collecting documents and then preparing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As the interventions of Judge Harhoff and Judge Delvoie have implied, the purpose of -- of a trial, even in cross-examination, is to move things forward. We -- we -- the -- how this last question about the method that he used in terms of doing his work as a journalist, and as Judge Harhoff has reminded you, we know that he's a journalist. The nature of the craft means that he synthesises material from a variety of sources and writes stories that his editor deem newsworthy. That's as far as it goes. How does it assist us, how does it move the matter forward, in terms of these -- these types of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was, Your Honour, exactly my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to put to Mr. Traynor actually that on the basis of the standards of your profession, of your work, I find that you are not balanced in your informations, that are you biased towards the Serbian, I would say, side, and that's why your articles are not accurately reflecting the situation in 1992 in Bosnia. Do you agree with me? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely disagree with you. I spend a lot of time in Serbia, in Belgrade, speaking to lots of people under the Milosevic years, from 1988 onwards. The biggest --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Please, Mr. Traynor --

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And speaking to lots of people in Belgrade, the human -- the democrats, the Djindjic people, Natasa Kandic, very brave human rights activists operating in Belgrade, getting a lot of information from them and reflecting that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. I agree with you that you collected lot of informations, but I am putting to you that you were actually disregard the golden rule of journalism in your work, and that is rule to get independent information from various independent sources from all -- at least two sides. I am putting to you that your work is seriously lacking objectivity and that's why that your articles could not be a source of any relevant assessment on information. Do you agree with me or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, you needn't answer that question. Mr. Pantelic, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't have further questions for this witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, I won't take up too much more of your time. Just a few questions in re-examination. Firstly, you may recall earlier today you were asked some questions about the number of people allegedly killed at the Vlasic mountain massacre and the interchange between you and Mr. Zupljanin during your interview with him, about the possible mistake, misinterpretation of those figures. Can you tell us, please, or do you recall who was doing the interpreting for you during that interview?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an -- I'm almost certain [Realtime transcript read in error "uncertain"] it was a police interpreter. It wasn't my regular interpreter in the -- the person that I had been working in Banja Luka who was a Bosnian Muslim and who wasn't comfortable going to the police building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, there's a correction to the transcript. It currently reads: "I'm uncertain it was a police interpreter." I think the witness said: "I'm fairly certain." Perhaps I can clarify that with him. If there's an issue.

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And your notes made at the time, which you read into the -- the transcript yesterday on this issue, and if I can just refresh your memory on that, you read -- you wrote down: "It is not the number you mentioned. Our information is about 50," you have written 50 in numbers not letters, "or more, but in the -- in this region the war is still on." And my question is, when you -- when you wrote, "It is not the number you mentioned," I'm assuming that you are writing down what Mr. Zupljanin is saying at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That note is -- I -- we have asked the question about the numbers that were circulated about the Vlasic massacre, which were in the region of 190, if I recall accurately, and we put that figure to him. What I have written down is his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall there being any issue at the time that that number 50 was a mistake or misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And taking into account your knowledge of the B/C/S language at the time, do you think would you have heard the difference, if the -- if the Mr. Zupljanin had said one number and the interpreter had said something else?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, having looked at -- seen the court documents that were up on the screen here an hour ago and the figure that is mentioned in the police documents of 140, there is -- there is an obvious correlation here. 140 plus 50 [Realtime transcript read in error "350"] is 190. So that is making me think that there was perhaps a misunderstanding or a mistranslation, but at the time, definitely not. And I was not alone, I was with a colleague, and we compare notes afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The colleague that you were with, she was from "The Washington Post"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did she make notes at the time as well?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And to your recollection, did she write any articles as a result of the interview that you did with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: She -- she wrote a fairly sizeable article on -- on the -- on the Vasic mountain incident. And she was really leading the questioning on this because she was working on that specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Just a correction to transcript. Page 54, line 13, instead of a figure 350, I believe witness said 50, because obviously 140 plus 350 is not 190. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Mr. Traynor, you will also recall being asked questions by my learned friend about the large article you wrote on the town of Kozarac and your -- your sources for that article, and the way that you gathered your information for that article. How long -- do you recall how long it took you to undertake that research?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, about a month, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you have a -- an overall focus or a theme for that article or were you writing it simply from a general specific?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, this was -- the destruction of Kozarac was already four or five months old and it was quite a large place, and it really had never been reported before and it was 15.000 civilians. And nobody knew what had happened there. It was quite an extraordinary thing. They was no basically minimal, unlike in the rest of Bosnia at the time and Sarajevo and other parts where you had aid convoys and UN and UNPROFOR troops, et cetera, there was no international witnesses in the Banja Luka region, in -- in the key months of May, June and July. So it struck me as a rather important subject, to try and research and recreate what happened to this basically -- almost 100 percent Muslim town on the main road of 50.000 civilians and what had happened to them. That was -- I only discovered it in the course of being there and then basically set about trying to establish what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And during this month of your research trying to establish what had happened, did you check with all available sources to you?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All available sources to me at the time, yes, mm-hm. I mean, I went to the police and couldn't get any further with the local Serb police and local Serb military.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked to recall or read through a list of articles that you had written in 1992, some of 170 articles, when Mr. Pantelic was putting to you that you weren't writing any articles about -- which had Serb victims in them. The list that you looked through only had the headings of the articles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this list here, yeah, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Have you actually read through all of those articles in the past few months?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sorry, no, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When would be the last time that you had reviewed your work from 1992?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. Not in living memory. Not that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you decided to permit this witness to testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter last year in October, part of his 92 ter package was a list of all of the articles that he wrote on the conflict in the former Yugoslavia from 1992 until 1995. It was a list of some 843 articles which had his byline and the heading and some of them had a -- the first sentence. That was part of the 92 ter package and put in by the Prosecution to show the -- the general background of his reporting and so forth throughout that time. It was specifically excluded by Your Honours in that ruling as being irrelevant and not necessary. In the circumstances, and in view of the fact that Mr. Pantelic has spent an enormous amount of time trying to allege a bias or some swaying of this journalist's viewpoint, I would submit that it is appropriate to reinstate that list, and Your Honours can, if necessary, review it for yourselves at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May we have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I make a short submission on that issue, Your Honour. Point number one, we discussed the matter of -- of -- of articles, sources, media sources, et cetera, before and Your Honour rules on that issue. I don't have any problem for Prosecution to locate -- I mean, what I said just was based on the danger or future for us to become a library of newspaper articles, video-clips, et cetera, from both sides, because it is a never-ending story and who knows how it will end at the end, how it will be finished. My point is, if Prosecution is sure, I don't have any problem to have only this particular article from 1992, from the list of 170, because it covers the -- the -- the time-frame of the indictment, if my friends can find and locate article with regard to the -- to the -- to the Serb victims and -- and -- and -- I don't have problem to tender that in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because there is no such article. That is my point. There is no. Whatever the title of the article, there is no. That is my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, have you finished your re-direct? Then let's deal with your requests by the end of the witness's testimony. So please finish up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked by my learned friend about how it came about that you were -- you came to interview Mr. Zupljanin. And you -- you said -- and the transcript is not quite clear on this, but you referred to a press service. Can you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm having difficulty recalling exactly, but, you know, anywhere you go you go to -- there was a press -- there was a spokesman, and we were at the Vance-Owen meeting with the assembled local Serbian political leadership and there would have been somebody dealing with the press there, and I don't remember who it was, and we would ask could we arrange some appointments. And that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you recall if you specifically asked to interview Mr. Zupljanin or was it a more general request?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more general.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you -- do you recall whether you asked -- qualified the general question in any way by nationality?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was a Serbian authority that we were -- you know, it would have been the mayor, it would have been the head of the party, the head of the police, military figures, people like Brdjanin, Vukic, and so on. And you know, these were the kind of people we were looking for to speak to -- to interview, and we were granted interview with Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you granted an interview with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, finally, when you were asked a question by Mr. Pantelic, just a few moments ago, about the events in Banja Luka, and the issue about why refugees were not returning to Bosnia, in answer you said, I'm not a sociologist. These were economic migrants leaving for a better life to get 400 Deutschemarks and stay in hotels. And then you said, Judging by what I see around me, I found this extremely inappropriate. Now can you just please expand and tell the Trial Chamber what you found extremely inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: IAN TRAYNOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had just been hearing lots of -- there was lots of people being uprooted. I mean, my colleague on the same newspaper had just spent three or four days walking through the hills, with convoys of refugees being kind of emptied out of that particular region south of Banja Luka, walking through front lines, civilians, women and children, and judging from what we were hearing from the UNHCR and ICRC, et cetera, there were dozens of buses and trucks on the move in that particular region at the moment, crossing front lines, getting turned back, going back, getting charged lots of money, getting their valuables taken away, et cetera, et cetera. So, you know, this is what one knew at the time, and to hear that basically these people were just looking for a better live and 400 Deutschemarks and a night in a German hotel was thoroughly perverse.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traynor, for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness. You're free to go and we wish you a safe return and/or onward journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, let us get back to the issue of admission into evidence of the 92 ter package. The Trial Chamber has discussed how we should deal with this, and our decision is that we will admit into evidence the two statements made by the witness in 1999 and 2000. And that's it. That is to say, that the 15 articles which were also part of the package will not be admitted into evidence. The reason is that we don't think that they have sufficient evidentiary value. They're interesting articles, they're good, but we wouldn't rely on them for the purpose of -- of -- of reaching our conclusions in the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution is not seeking to tender those as truth of the contents so -- the back-door approach that Mr. O'Sullivan alluded to yesterday. The Prosecution is seeking to tender them as -- as the writings of this witness to provide you with the insight into what was happening from his perspective at the time, as a journalist on the ground, and -- and as an example of the media reporting in at the time. And as you are aware, the media played a large role in Bosnia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are fully aware of it. We have Mr. Traynor's testimony and we now have the two statements, and that will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a real difficulty with this and it's one I raised at the beginning of the case, that we really need to know, at the beginning, what is to be admitted as part of the 92 ter package and what is not. Because if we don't know -- if we'd known that was going to be your view, we would have gone into a much grater detail about these articles and the information that was contained in them because it's the notice that is being given to -- apart from any other context of the articles, to those who are engaged in this conflict about what the reporting was. And there's evidence already, and there will be further evidence, that the international reporting was of some importance to those who -- I imagine all sides in this conflict. But it's the principle of it, Your Honours. And I did raise this some time ago. We need to know at the beginning whether a package, a 92 ter package is admitted or not. And that's the whole idea. And indeed my understanding was that the ruling -- sorry, may I finish. I apologise, but may I finish. Your ruling was the package was admitted. Yes, on -- so, I mean, that's what -- if we have a ruling that a 92 ter -- that a witness may be 92 ter, a witness may be admitted under the 92 ter package, we assume that the exhibits go with it; or if not, then we should be told at the time which exhibits are not going in. May I say it is unfair, otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you assist me Ms. Korner. You indicated that we -- the application would have been made at the time when -- in respect of this -- the 92 ter package relating to this witness would have only been made when this witness -- when this person became a witness and we specifically reserve that question. So I'm -- perhaps I'm -- I'm misunderstanding you when you say that we would have ruled on the admission of the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honours say -- Your Honours deferred a decision on the 92 ter package until cross-examination had finished which is -- you have done it occasionally with some witnesses and not with others, so at the moment it is not always the same practice. And I raised some time ago, I think right at the first witness, that we should know at the beginning of the examination-in-chief, which is based, at the moment -- and the time we ask for is based on the admission of the statement or the interview and the documents that go with it, unless we're specifically told, in advance, we will not admit those documents. Now, had we known that, in this case, Your Honours would have ruled inadmissible all the articles, we would have gone into -- certainly we'd have listed all the articles so it is on the transcript. We might have gone into some detail. So we're at a disadvantage from this ruling.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: With respect, Ms. Korner, I'm not sure that I appreciate - and the fault may be entirely mine - why, in the OTP's view, the result is unfair. Inasmuch as Ms. Pidwell has said that the accompanying documents were not being sought to be tendered as proof of the truth of the contents but merely of the fact that they were made, but inasmuch as the -- whatever role the press would have played in the course of conflict is not subject of the inquiry by this Chamber, the -- I don't see how that -- the fact that this particular -- the witness just released would have written a number of articles moves the matter forward, and for that reason, I'm not sure that I follow how the OTP feels that it is prejudiced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the main -- or a main issue in this case is going to be the knowledge and notification which the two accused, in particular, had in this case. Articles which were published by members of the international press were brought to the attention, we know that, we've heard evidence about it, of the various -- the leadership in this case if you like. That's one of the reasons that prompted, eventually in August, the major outcry over the camps which prompted the investigations which Your Honours have seen. And the giving of notice -- and indeed these articles themselves, although they are hearsay, they're first-hand hearsay. In other words, that the -- the -- the author has spoken to the various people that he says he has spoken to and they are admissible as directly going to some of the major events in this case. And you've heard from the journalist. It is suggested that he heard only one side. That is a matter Your Honours will take into account. But, Your Honour, the articles themselves -- I'm sorry, there are -- which is a separate issue from giving notice to us of what is going to be admitted or not, but is a separate issue that those articles in themselves, such as they are, given the weight that he has spoken to only limited numbers of people, are admissible evidence and have been as admissible evidence in many cases. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, there is -- in the ruling that we have just given, there is no principle position that would suggest that the Chamber will not admit any article, newspaper article. In fact, I think we have already admitted quite a few. The Chamber's point is that what needs to be on the record for the purpose of the Prosecution in relation to the point that you have just raised, namely, to -- to -- to show that the international press was writing about the events and that this information was being brought to the accused by way of the international press coverage, is clearly on the record, so we don't think that it is necessary to admit into evidence the articles that have you included in your 65 ter package. In -- to show that extra point. And as Ms. Pidwell said and the Presiding Judge reminded you, the articles anyway weren't brought for their contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I heard Ms. Pidwell say that, Your Honour, and I don't like to -- to disagree with a member of my own team. But I actually I do think it does have an element of that -- I don't think. What I think is irrelevant, as I keep pointing out. We would submit that it is also, although it is hearsay evidence, it is admissible for the truth of the contents. But, Your Honours -- but can I return to my original point which is the fact that we respectfully say to Your Honours that we should be notified at the beginning of the -- the evidence of a witness, where he is a 92 ter, he or she is a 92 ter witness, what is going to be admitted and what is not because if is not going to be admitted at the end of -- when we have no chance to go back over it, in respect of documents, then we would probably go into more detail. And, Your Honours, in rulings you have given, you've indicated where you've excluded documents before this. And no indication was given with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't think that admitting a 92 ter witness means admitting the 92 ter package you propose. And we've always said, in numerous decisions, that it is after having heard the witness, that we will determine in what way, and if the documents on your proposed 92 ter list are supporting the statement. And that's the 92 ter Rule. It has to be supporting the documents. Well, we consider that these articles are not supporting the statement. And it's the statement that is what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course -- and of course, Your Honour, I'm not suggesting for one moment that Your Honours are not entitled to take that view. And you've heard my arguments and you don't accept them, that's -- and I'm not seeking to [indiscernible] that. What I'm talking about now is giving us notice through the rulings that you make, as you have done, as to what you consider to be inextricably linked and what not, what you will admit out of the document packages. And I think out of fairness we should be entitled to know that before we examine in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, you had something to offer on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very briefly and I believe we can go back. Probably the first witness where this arose was Djeric, going back to last October. In our submission, the position that Judge Delvoie has just enunciated is the practice we have been following, that the witness comes, and where there are times or certain documents where it may be contentious whether or not they should be admitted, those decisions are made by the Chamber following direct and cross. So we have been following this practice at least since Djeric. That is my first recollection, maybe earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I would add to that that to the extent that it appears that that position is exceptional, the easy explanation is that the -- where the 92 ter -- where there is obviously no controversy about the 92 ter package accompanying -- the package accompanying a 92 ter witness, then we needn't go through this exercise. And it really only arises where it is necessary to look at the question, and as Mr. O'Sullivan has said, as Judge Delvoie has reminded, that we have -- this is the practice that we have followed and, quite frankly, I see no other way in dealing with it but to examine where there is a controversy, it -- on a case-by-case basis, and it would be well-nigh impossible, perhaps impossible is putting it too high, but I don't see how we could do it beforehand, as you -- you -- you are suggesting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's -- can I go back to Mr. O'Sullivan's intervention in this. The point about us filing a motion, saying here is the package and here are the documents and the Defence response is that the Defence are not meant to leave it, as I pointed out yesterday, until the witness is here and waiting to give evidence, and then not give any notice at all properly to the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber. It is meant to respond saying it objects. And at that stage both Your Honours and the Prosecution are on notice. The Defence did not do so, as I've already said twice now, in this particular case. And, Your Honours, I think it would have been only right and fair that we should have been given advance notification and, as I say, it is likely that we would have taken a different course with this witness. So that is the only point I am making. So Your Honours, I'm asking that in future, in particular with the witness who's coming tomorrow, particularly as he's on video-line, that if there is to be any objection taken from the Defence to any of the documents that are in the package, we should be notified no later than 4.00 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I think that is as far as we can take this matter now. We would -- Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I terribly apologise. If you are going to adjourn now, or we are sitting still, ten minutes. That's just my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think there was anything left for us to deal with, but if you have a matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour. I would really ask for your attention. Yesterday at the end of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. The -- the -- such of the 92 ter packages we have admitted as has been tendered -- as we have admitted would now be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And they shall be admitted in a package as Exhibit P01356.01 until .17. Thank you, Your Honours. I shall repeat that the 92 ter package of --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will make that correction. The two statements shall be admitted as Exhibit P01356.01 and P01356.02. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yesterday when I was conferring with my client, my learned friend Mr. Krgovic was very precise and he made a submission with regard to adjudicated facts issue. And I take it it is not completed so I just have a few remarks with that regard which might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In addition what my learned friends Mr. Zecevic, Mr. O'Sullivan, and Mr. Krgovic said on that topic, I would like to -- to -- to add the following submission. Your Honours, the -- the -- I mean, my understanding of -- of Article, I believe, it's 94(B) which is related to judicial notice, is that by all means in terms of judicial economy, in terms of efficiency of trial, certain standards must apply and finally we have a case law within the Tribunal with that regard, so on and so forth. My -- actually the Zupljanin Defence position is the following. This approach should be taken only in very limited occasions. I will give you example. We have Srebrenica case. Srebrenica case started with case against General Krstic, then against the other number of accused so-called Srebrenica 1. Now we have Srebrenica 2. Also we a case Sarajevo bombing campaign relating to General Galic and General Milosevic. We also have a Prijedor number of cases, starting from Dusko Tadic, then Chief of Crisis Staff Stakic, and then number of officers guards, in the camps. My point is the following. Yes, I could personally agree in order to speed up proceedings to follow certain judicial economy standards but only for these kind of limited groups of cases. Yes, it was applicable to certain extent subject to conditions; for example, for Srebrenica, or for Sarajevo, or for Prijedor. But here, we don't have a previous case specifically related to a high-ranked police officials; I'm speaking on behalf of Mr. Zupljanin. For example, you would have previous case against his associate or his, I don't know, deputy, then certain findings on that basis could -- could, as I said, reach that standard, to be -- to be assessed as adjudicated facts. So my point is, when you asked me what is my position - bless you, Your Honour - what is my position with regard to -- what is the Defence position with regard to adjudicated facts. I said on the basis of what I just said, I'm objecting. And my learned friend Mr. Krgovic was very efficient showing you, for example, in Tesic case, how in fact adjudicated facts principle is -- is -- is relative and that we have to -- to go from case to case to know what we are going -- what we should challenge or not. I can give you example. I think it was Judge Harhoff or Judge Delvoie asking me do I challenge, for example, census for Teslic, figures about the demographic census in 1991. I said yes. I'm challenging that. On which basis? On the following basis: Number one, it is beyond the scope of the indictment because that was the census in 1991. And then this particular fact does not consist another aspect, which is the number of workers, I mean, three nationalities, for example, in Teslic, working abroad, and they are appearing in the census but actually they are not there. So that -- that's the point why we are challenging this kind of fact, and we were quite successful in -- in against Ewa Tabeau, demographic expert, in Samac case because, you know, that was dismissed. Her demographic study was completely dismissed as absolutely irrelevant to the case. Now, I am going back, Your Honours, to the fundamental issue of this case. This is a case on the basis of Prosecution theory which is abbreviation of JCE, which is just convict everyone, which calls joint criminal enterprise. With this kind of theory, I am absolutely entitled to challenge even -- I don't know, a minor fact of -- of -- of certain perpetrator in -- in certain area because this broad theory which is -- which is advocated by the OTP is such that even -- even this adjudicated fact goes to the legal issues. Because the point is that -- that such a broad theory is going to provoke reaction, in terms of challenging certain adjudicated facts, based on the legal issue. Because, you know, these standards person A, B, C, sees not a part of JCE of where A and B are, and then principal perpetrator D is acting and so and so forth. I mean, this is absolutely messy, messy theory. What is our position? Our position, Your Honours, is that we are -- we are actually -- we are actually -- and Judge Harhoff, being presiding Pre-Trial Judge may -- may correct me if I am wrong. It was during -- during one of the Pre-Trial Conference in June 2009. In order to be efficient and in order to avoid -- you asked me, Judge Harhoff, whether I will accept certain adjudicated fact. I said yes. I will accept many of them, but only in the case where this umbrella crime theory catch them all, whole JCE advocated by the OTP will be -- will be -- will be set aside. I am ready to admit number of adjudicated facts, only if this Office of the Prosecution will follow well-established practice of the ICC Court on the basis of civil law jurisdiction and the principles and enshrined in the principle of co-perpetration through control. That's the theory that I'm -- just five seconds, Your Honour. That's a theory that I'm, if they will plead this theory, will accept certain adjudicated facts. Why? Because they have to show whether my client was in which kind of relation and nexus to consequences and to principal perpetrators. Not to say simply no, you have trouble here, you have members of army, you have a civilian aspect, you have a guard, you have officers. You're responsible for natural and foreseeable consequences. No, Your Honour. We have to go to get back to the real and proper and fair standards. And I must say that, that I'm very happy -- I'm not sure that I'm right, but that Honourable Judge Agius, who was quite, I would say, he was -- he was an excellent Judge, found in Brdjanin discussing the issue of JCE in Brdjanin case that now he is sitting on Appeals Chamber so we have some lights even on that part of theory that a certain -- that certain legal minds will -- will take care about the limitations and the dangerous aspect of JCE, which is advocated by the OTP in such a broad terms. Thank you very much for your attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic, for your assistance. Ms. Pidwell, we're past the hour of adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I know, sir, I have 20 seconds on an issue raised by Judge Harhoff yesterday, the date of the Kozarac video. I have that information if Your Honours would like that now. The last video tendered by the Prosecution was first aired -- it's P1360, was first aired on British television on the 3rd of February, 1993, and that was verified by the British Film Institute library.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And so we rise to reconvene tomorrow in Courtroom III, at 2.15 in the afternoon.
